lesson.title: Spreadsheets in Plain Text: Reading and Writing CSV Files
lesson.summary: CSV (comma-separated values) files store tabular data as plain text, and Python's csv module handles the tricky parsing details, like commas inside a value, so you do not have to write fragile split(",") code yourself.
lesson.body:
You already know how to open a file and read its contents, and you know how to use a string's split() method to break a line into pieces at some separator character. CSV format takes exactly that idea and turns it into a real, widely used standard. CSV stands for "comma-separated values," and a CSV file is just a plain text file where each line is one row of data and a comma separates the values within that row. Open a CSV file in a plain text editor and you will see something like name,score on the first line and Amara,92 on the next. No special software is required to read it, because it is nothing more than text, and that simplicity is exactly why CSV has survived for decades as the default way spreadsheets, gradebooks, and databases hand data to each other.

It is tempting to think you could just read each line and call line.split(",") to pull out the values, and for very simple data that works. Real data breaks this quickly, though. What happens when a value itself contains a comma, like a name written "Smith, John" or an address field "Springfield, IL"? A properly formatted CSV file wraps that value in quotation marks so a comma inside the quotes does not count as a separator, and it also has rules for what to do if a quotation mark needs to appear inside a quoted value. Writing that quoting and escaping logic by hand is fiddly and easy to get wrong, so Python ships a csv module that already gets it right, and you should reach for it instead of split() any time you are working with real CSV data.

Here is a complete round trip: writing a small CSV file with a header row, then reading it back.

```python
import csv

with open("grades.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["name", "score"])
    writer.writerow(["Amara", 92])
    writer.writerow(["Liam", 78])

with open("grades.csv", "r", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
```

This prints:

```
['name', 'score']
['Amara', '92']
['Liam', '78']
```

Notice two things. First, csv.writer() takes a list for each row, which is the same list type you have already been building and looping over. Second, and this trips up almost every beginner at least once, '92' in the output is a string, not the int 92 you wrote. CSV is a text format, so every single value that comes back from csv.reader() is a str, even if it looks like a number. If you want to do arithmetic with a score, you must convert it yourself with int() or float() before using it. The newline="" argument in both open() calls is a small but important detail the csv module asks for: without it, Windows systems can insert extra blank lines between rows, because both the csv module and the text mode newline translation would otherwise try to handle line endings at the same time.

When a CSV file has a header row, as this one does, you often do not want to remember that column 0 is the name and column 1 is the score. csv.DictReader() reads the first row as the set of column names and then hands you each remaining row as a dictionary mapping those names to that row's values.

```python
with open("grades.csv", "r", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row["name"], "scored", row["score"])
```

This prints:

```
Amara scored 92
Liam scored 78
```

There is a matching csv.DictWriter() for writing rows out from dictionaries, using the same idea in reverse. CSV is the right tool whenever your data is naturally a flat table, a fixed set of columns repeated over many rows. When your data has more structure than that, like a list nested inside a record, or a record nested inside another record, you need a format built for that shape, which is exactly what the next chapter introduces.
